text: Once we were safely ashore, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The islanders showed us unusual kindness. They lit a fire and welcomed all of us, because it was raining and cold.
Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and was putting them on the fire when a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened itself on his hand.
When the islanders saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to one another, This man must be a murderer. He escaped the sea, but justice will not let him live.
Paul, however, shook the snake off into the fire and suffered no harm.
The people expected him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead, but after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and began saying he was a god.
Nearby were the estates of the island's chief official, a man named Publius. He welcomed us and entertained us kindly for three days.
His father was sick in bed with fever and dysentery. Paul went to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
When this happened, the rest of the island's sick came as well and were healed.
They honored us greatly, and when we were ready to sail, they supplied us with everything we needed.
After three months we set sail on a ship from Alexandria that had wintered at the island, whose figurehead was the Twin Gods.
We put in at Syracuse and stayed there three days.
From there we sailed on and arrived at Rhegium. The next day a south wind came up, and on the day after that we reached Puteoli.
There we found some believers who invited us to stay with them a week. And so we went on toward Rome.
When the believers in Rome heard we were coming, they came out to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and was encouraged.
When we entered Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier assigned to guard him.

Three days later Paul called together the local Jewish leaders. When they had gathered, he said: Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or our customs, I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.
After questioning me, they wanted to set me free, since they found no charge against me deserving death.
But when the Jewish leaders objected, I was forced to appeal to Caesar, not because I have any accusation to bring against my own people.
That is why I asked to see you and speak with you: it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.
They replied, We have received no letters from Judea about you, and none of our people who have come here has reported anything bad about you.
But we want to hear what you believe, for we know that people everywhere speak against this sect.

So they arranged a day to meet with him, and many came to the place where he was staying. From morning until evening he explained and testified about the kingdom of God, trying to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some were convinced by what he said, but others would not believe.
They left disagreeing among themselves, after Paul had made this final statement: The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through the prophet Isaiah when he said to your ancestors,
Go to this people and say, You will hear and hear but never understand, you will look and look but never see.

For this people's heart has grown calloused, their ears are hard of hearing, and they have closed their eyes, so that they might not see with their eyes or hear with their ears or understand with their heart and turn back so that I could heal them.
Therefore I want you to know that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.
For two years Paul stayed in his own rented house and welcomed everyone who came to see him.
He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness, and no one stopped him.
